==Problem==
A cart rolls down a hill, travelling <imath>5</imath> inches the first second and accelerating so that during each successive <imath>1</imath>-second time interval, it travels <imath>7</imath> inches more than during the previous <imath>1</imath>-second interval. The cart takes <imath>30</imath> seconds to reach the bottom of the hill. How far, in inches, does it travel?

<imath>\textbf{(A)} ~215 \qquad\textbf{(B)} ~360\qquad\textbf{(C)} ~2992\qquad\textbf{(D)} ~3195\qquad\textbf{(E)} ~3242</imath>

==Solution 1 (Arithmetic Series)==
Since <cmath>\mathrm{Distance}=\mathrm{Speed}\cdot\mathrm{Time},</cmath> we seek the sum <cmath>5\cdot1+12\cdot1+19\cdot1+26\cdot1+\cdots=5+12+19+26+\cdots,</cmath> in which there are <imath>30</imath> terms.

The last term is <imath>5+7\cdot(30-1)=208.</imath> Therefore, the requested sum is <cmath>5+12+19+26+\cdots+208=\frac{5+208}{2}\cdot30=\boxed{\textbf{(D)} ~3195}.</cmath> Recall that to find the sum of an arithmetic series, we take the average of the first and last terms and then multiply by the number of terms: <cmath>\mathrm{Sum}=\frac{\mathrm{First}+\mathrm{Last}}{2}\cdot\mathrm{Count}.</cmath> ~MRENTHUSIASM

==Solution 2 (Arithmetic Series)==
The distance (in inches) traveled within each <imath>1</imath>-second interval is: <cmath>5,5+1(7),5+2(7), \dots , 5+29(7).</cmath>
This is an arithmetic sequence so the total distance travelled, found by summing them up is:
<cmath>\text{number of terms} \cdot \text{average of terms} = \text{number of terms} \cdot \dfrac{\text{first term}+\text{last term}}{2}.</cmath>
Or, <cmath>30 \cdot \dfrac{5+5+29(7)}{2} = 15 \cdot 213 = \boxed{\textbf{(D)} ~3195}.</cmath>
~BakedPotato66

==Solution 3 (Answer Choices and Modular Arithmetic)==
From the <imath>30</imath>-term sum <cmath>5+12+19+26+\cdots</cmath> in Solution 1, taking modulo <imath>10</imath> gives <cmath>5+12+19+26+\cdots \equiv 3\cdot(5+2+9+6+3+0+7+4+1+8) = 3\cdot45\equiv5 \pmod{10}.</cmath> The only answer choices congruent to <imath>5</imath> modulo <imath>10</imath> are <imath>\textbf{(A)}</imath> and <imath>\textbf{(D)}.</imath> By a quick estimation, <imath>\textbf{(A)}</imath> is too small, leaving us with <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)} ~3195}.</imath> 

~MRENTHUSIASM

==Solution 4 (Motion With Constant Acceleration)==

This problem can be solved by physics method. This method is perhaps the quickest too and shows the beauty of the problem. The average speed increases <imath>7 \ \text{in/s}</imath> per second. So, the acceleration <imath>a=7 \ \text{in/s\textsuperscript{2}}.</imath> The average speed of the first second is <imath>5 \ \text{in/s}.</imath> We can know the initial velocity <imath>v_0=5-0.5\cdot7=1.5.</imath> (Because of the formula for the distance traveled in the <imath>k</imath>th one-second interval being <imath>\Delta x_k = v_0 + a\left(k - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)</imath>). The displacement at <imath>t=30</imath> is <cmath>s=\frac{1}{2}at^2+v_0t=\frac{1}{2}\cdot7\cdot30^2+1.5\cdot30= \boxed{\textbf{(D)} ~3195}.</cmath>
~Bran_Qin
